# The Tuesday Afternoon That Wasn't, and the Ones That Were

There is a particular quality to the world on a Wednesday in November that no one has ever decided to name. The sky is that low, diffuse gray that isn't quite rain but also isn't quite not-rain, a held breath suspended over the whole of the earth. The light comes from everywhere and from no direction, as if it's been diffused through a very large and very tired window. The air smells like wet leaves that will never quite be picked up, and like the particular cold of metal, and like something from your childhood you can't quite retrieve because the name is on the tip of your mouth and then it's gone.

I want to talk about these hours. Not the ones that get written in memoirs, not the ones that make good material for a podcast, but the ones that are just... there. The ones where you sit in a kitchen and make pasta from scratch and the water boils and you stand there too long watching it boil, and the pasta water is going to be fine, of course, but you're standing there watching it boil, and the light in the kitchen has shifted to that slightly greenish afternoon quality, and you think, *I'm making dinner for one person*, and the sentence is completely ordinary and completely true and completely enough.

The thing is, most people spend the vast majority of their adult lives in exactly this condition. Not the dramatic condition. Not the defining condition. The condition of Tuesday. The condition of doing the dishes after dinner and noticing that the water is warm in a way it shouldn't be and turning off the tap. The condition of walking to the mailbox and reading nothing. The condition of lying down in the evening and staring at the ceiling not out of depression, exactly, but out of a kind of gentle, bone-deep *finishedness*, a sense that whatever small work today required of you has been completed, and there is nothing more to do.

And I think this is the most radical fact of human experience, and also the least discussed. We build our entire cultural apparatus around the exceptional. We have language for the peak experience, for the crisis, for the transformation. We have *epiphany*. We have *the moment everything changed*. We have movies about a single Tuesday that is not a normal Tuesday. We have novels that span decades only to deliver their real content in the final page. The architecture of storytelling is structured around the interruption of the ordinary. The ordinary is the setting. The ordinary is the waiting room. You don't get to stay in the waiting room, because then the story stops.

But if you strip the story away, if you strip the exception away, what remains is the ordinary. And it is not a small thing to remain. It is the whole thing. It is the substrate. It is what your life is actually made of, the way a tree is mostly the part you can't see beneath the soil.

I remember an afternoon, a few years ago, sitting on the back porch with a glass of iced tea that had gone completely flat. It was early September and the kind of heat had settled over everything that made your shirt stick to your back in a way that felt like a mild, damp embrace. A dog was lying on the grass at the end of the driveway, one front paw lifted off the concrete and resting on the grass, in that particular pose that dogs adopt when they have decided they are no longer in a hurry to do anything. I watched the dog. The dog did not perform. The dog did not do a trick for me. The dog simply was, in the heat, with one paw in the grass, breathing in a way I can describe as slow and unbothered.

And something shifted in me that I can only describe as a kind of recognition. Not a revelation. Not a breakthrough. A recognition, like recognizing a face in a crowd, except the face was my own, and it was the face of a person who had simply decided to exist for an afternoon without producing or consuming or accomplishing anything that could be pointed at later and said, *See what I did?*

The dog's ear twitched. A bird moved from one branch to another in the yard, a movement so small I might have missed it. The iced tea sweated down the glass and a little puddle was forming on the wooden slat of the porch where my hand was. I felt warm. I felt warm and I felt like nothing was required of me. And the nothing was not an absence. It was not a void to be filled. It was a kind of fullness, but a fullness of a different species than the fullness of having just received good news or finished a task or seen something beautiful. It was the fullness of a room that is simply occupied. Of a body that is simply here.

I think about how strange it is that we need an exception to feel that our experience has value. If I had told you that I had sat on a porch for two hours and watched a dog lie in the grass and felt warm and felt nothing required of me, you would probably feel a little... thin, right? A little *what*? You would want to know if something happened. Did the dog bark at something? Did you meet someone? Did the light change in some way that was meaningful? Did you have a thought? A vision? A sudden, clarifying insight about your mother or your career or the nature of time?

And if I said no, if I said the only thing that happened was that the tea went flat and the light moved slowly across the porch boards, you might say, okay, but that's not *the* afternoon. That's not *a* story. And maybe you'd be right in the narrow sense. But I don't know how to reconcile that with the fact that those are the afternoons I remember most vividly, years later. Not the ones where something dramatic occurred, but the ones where I was just... warm. Just sitting. Just watching the dog's ear twitch. Just there.

There's a concept in Japanese aesthetics called *ma*. It's been translated as "negative space" or "pause" or "emptiness," but I think those translations actually flatten it. *Ma* is not emptiness. It is the space *between*, and it is not empty. It is the space where the sound of the koto string lingers after it has been plucked. It is the silence between two notes of music that gives the music its shape. Without the *ma*, the music is just a pile of sounds. The *ma* is what makes it music.

I think most of our adult lives are *ma*. The space between the accomplishments. The silence between the dramatic beats. And I think we spend a huge amount of energy trying to fill the *ma*, trying to fill every pause with something that can be justified, something that produces a result, something that moves the needle. We fill it with our phones. We fill it with scrolling. We fill it with podcasts and news and the anxious management of content intake. We fill it because the silence terrifies us, because the unoccupied minute feels like a personal failure, like a waste of something that was lent to us on loan and is now accruing interest.

But what if the *ma* is the point? What if the whole point of the life is the *ma*? What if the events are just the strings being plucked, and the actual music is everything around them?

I've been thinking about this in relation to the way we talk about other people's lives. We talk about the achievements. The promotion. The house. The trip. The pregnancy. The diagnosis. The death. The recovery. The argument that changed the marriage. The conversation that broke the friendship. We talk about the peaks and the valleys and the turning points. And this is fine. This is not nothing. But it is like describing a piece of music by listing the notes. The notes are real. The notes are not nothing. But the music is not the notes. The music is the shape, the rhythm, the *ma*, the way one note leans toward the next.

A person's life is not a sequence of events. It is a texture. It is the quality of the Tuesdays. It is the way the light came in the kitchen while they made pasta. It is the particular sound of their footsteps on the kitchen tile, the sound of the tap running, the sound of the dog at the end of the driveway breathing slowly in the heat. It is the quality of their attention. It is how they were there, in the unremarkable hours, in the hours where nothing was required of them, whether they were there fully or whether they were somewhere else, in the phone, in the past, in a mental rehearsal of a conversation that hadn't happened yet.

And here's the thing that I find genuinely difficult to say without sounding self-important: I think the capacity to be present in an unremarkable moment is one of the most advanced things a person can do. Not a spiritual advancement. Not a mystical breakthrough. Just the capacity to stand in front of the boiling water and watch it boil, and to feel that this is not a waste of time, and to feel that this is the whole of the task. To not be in a hurry to get to the next thing. To not be in a hurry to get to the thing that will justify your experience. Just to be here. Just to be warm. Just to be there.

I think this is why so much of what we consume is designed to prevent this. We are given content that moves us faster than we can be still. We are given narratives that require a resolution. We are given social media feeds that are essentially, *look what someone else is experiencing right now, now what are you experiencing, why aren't you experiencing something*, and the whole architecture of modern life is built on the premise that if you are not experiencing an exception, you are failing. You are missing out. You are behind. You are wasting the afternoon.

And I get it. I do. The pressure is real. The expectation is not nothing. When you are young, when you are building, when you are trying to prove that you exist and that your existence matters, the pressure to produce is almost physiological. It is the pressure of being alive in a world that rewards motion. And I think that phase is necessary. I don't think anyone should be told to sit on a porch while they are twenty-two and desperately trying to figure out who they are. The *ma* has a later chapter, or maybe it is the chapter that keeps coming back.

But I think what gets lost is the permission. The permission to be a Tuesday. The permission to be the unremarkable. The permission to have an afternoon where the only thing that happened was that you were warm and the tea went flat and a dog moved one paw from the concrete to the grass and you watched it do so and felt, not thrilled, not inspired, not enlightened, but simply... satisfied. And by satisfied I don't mean contentment in the smug, self-satisfied way. I mean the satisfaction of a hunger that was actually full. The satisfaction of having been given exactly what you needed and nothing more. The satisfaction of a body that has completed its small work of being a body in the heat and can now rest.

There is a particular kind of loneliness in a world that values the exception. It is the loneliness of realizing that the most common mode of your experience, the mode you have been living in since you were born, is the mode that no one talks about. You spend most of your life in the *ma*, and then you are expected to perform as if the *ma* is a waiting room, as if you are always just waiting for the music to start, when really the *ma* is the music, and the notes are just little interruptions.

I think about all the afternoons I've had that I will never write about. All the afternoons where I drove somewhere and the radio played a song and I liked the song and I didn't write it down because it wasn't the *song*. All the evenings where I read something and it was fine, just fine, not important, and I folded the newspaper or closed the book and the lights dimmed outside and I thought, *well, that was fine*. And "fine" is doing a lot of work in that sentence. Fine is not nothing. Fine is not an empty container. Fine is the quality of a thing that is adequate, that is sufficient, that meets the need. Fine is the quality of the afternoon where nothing was required and nothing was lacking.

And maybe the whole project of a life, if there is a project, is to be more often *fine*. To be more often *fine* in the way the dog is fine, in the way the tea is fine, in the way the light is fine as it moves across the kitchen wall. To be fine without needing to be extraordinary. To be a Tuesday and not a Tuesday that is also a movie.

I don't know if that's right. I don't know if it's what anyone wants to hear, or if it's even coherent. But I think it's true. I think the unremarkable is the whole. I think the Tuesday is the life. I think the dog in the grass is not a metaphor for anything, and that's the point. I think the tea going flat is not an allegory for the impermanence of youth or the fading of summer, and that's also the point. I think the fact that it means nothing beyond what it is, that it is simply tea, simply flat, simply going flat, is the deepest thing about it.

And I think there is a kindness in that. A kindness in the fact that you don't have to produce anything. A kindness in the fact that you can be a Tuesday and that is not a failure. A kindness in the fact that the light in the kitchen can be slightly greenish and you can stand in front of the boiling water and not be in a hurry. A kindness in the fact that the dog can lift one paw from the concrete to the grass and that is not a story, and you can watch it happen, and the watching can be the whole of the afternoon, and the whole of the afternoon can be enough.

I think. I mean, I think, which is to say I'm not sure. I'm not going to resolve this in the next few hundred words. I'm not going to give you a punchline. I'm not going to make it into a fable or a parable or a little story with a moral tucked in the last line where I say, *and the dog learned nothing and that was the lesson*.

I'm just going to sit here for a minute, in the space between what I was going to say and what I actually said, and the space is fine. The space is fine. And the space is the whole.

And the light is moving across the wall, and it's slightly greenish, and no one is in a hurry.

And the dog, wherever it is, somewhere in a yard, is fine.
